achieved.baseline_gap_note: This reaches minority-class F1 well below the published 0.6323 (GFP+XGBoost, AMLworld HI-Small, NeurIPS 2023 D&B). The cause is a feature ARCHITECTURE difference, not a tuning one: the gap is unreachable at any threshold, because measured AUPRC is far below what that F1 requires. IBM's Graph Feature Preprocessor computes per-transaction subgraph patterns over a dynamically updated graph; this project computes per-account scalar aggregates. A degree is one number per account, whereas a GFP feature is a pattern match in that transaction's own neighbourhood at the moment it arrives. GFP ships in `snapml` under a Proprietary licence and is excluded by this project's commercial-OK-only rule, but the licence is not itself the cause - the architecture is, and it is reimplementable without `snapml`, simply at more cost than renaming aggregates. Reachability is computed to 4 hops against injected CYCLE attempts of up to 10; that was previously recorded as a main cause and is NOT one - the GFP paper (arXiv:2402.08593) decomposes its own contribution and caps multi-hop cycle and scatter-gather features at about 4% relative, while fan-in/fan-out, which is reimplemented here, carries more than 30%. The evaluation is strictly inductive and temporally split. Per-account aggregates are causal (each row sees only edges strictly before it); the structural block - cycle closure, scatter-gather, bank diversity, burst degree - is still fitted on the training window, because recomputing sparse reachability at every timestep is not tractable here. Reported as measured; not adjusted to close the gap. Full workings: references/finance-gap-investigation.md.

calibration.does_not_move_ranking: Platt is STRICTLY monotone, so AUC and AUC-PR are unchanged by construction: measured Round 49, both are identical to the uncalibrated values to ten decimals, and that held for the map fitted on the probability and for the logit(s) map that now ships alike. The qualifier matters and was missing - isotonic is only WEAKLY monotone, and on this same split it moved AUROC by -0.00031674 and AUPRC by -0.01121590 (-9.09%). Calibration by a strictly monotone map fixes what a probability MEANS, never how the rows are ordered. ONE HONEST QUALIFIER ON THE MAP THAT SHIPS: logit() clips at 1e-12, so scores below 1e-12 or above 1-1e-12 would tie. None exist on this split (the raw range is 4.4e-11 to 0.99997), so no pair is tied and the AUCs above are exact; a retrain that saturates a leaf would need this re-checked rather than assumed.
calibration.fitted_on: validation split; scored on the held-out test split
calibration.formula: p = 1 / (1 + exp(a * logit(clip(score, logit_clip_eps, 1 - logit_clip_eps)) + b)), logit(q) = log(q / (1 - q))
calibration.reliability_diagram_defensible_here: YES on this split, and the first draft of this note said the opposite. Riley et al. (Stat Med 2021) put the floor for a flexible calibration curve at about 200 events; this test split carries 2,321. The 164-event figure this project quotes elsewhere is the 2D OVERLAY payload (8,192 sampled rows at a 0.02 base rate), not the test split, and carrying it over here would have declined a curve that the data supports - the same wrong-denominator mistake this repository already documents under 'ask what the metric was divided by'. The floor genuinely does bind on medical (about 42 events) and satellite (about 113). The CORP terms below are reported regardless, because PAV picks no bin count and so they are stable where a binned curve is not.
calibration.why_not_isotonic: MEASURED Round 49 on this split, not argued: isotonic Brier 0.00142218 / log-loss 0.00820025 against 0.00142199 / 0.00818964 for the same fit_platt fed logit(s) - within noise on both proper scoring rules, so ICML 2005's 'as good as, or better than' holds here in the 'as good as' form. Platt is kept on the tie-break: isotonic is only WEAKLY monotone, collapsed 1,388,669 distinct scores to 138, and cost AUROC 0.00031674 and AUPRC 0.01121590 (-9.09%), while both Platt arms moved neither to ten decimals; it also emitted exactly 0 on 464,176 test rows, one a true positive, and 138 breakpoints are not two floats a browser can apply. ONE CORRECTION TO THE OLD REASONING SURVIVES HERE: the calibration set carries 801 events, not 2,321 (that is the test split). The second - that a/b were fitted on a PROBABILITY rather than a log-odds, making the map return 0.00090148 for nine of ten deciles - is FIXED, not outstanding: on_logit is true above and the map published here is the logit(s) arm those numbers describe. Workings: references/finance-calibration-isotonic-vs-platt.md.

not_measured.published_source: PGS Catalog PPM001647 for PGS000004 (PRS313): AUROC 0.633 (95% CI 0.624-0.641), n=400,812 Europeans - 4,340 cases and 396,472 controls - from Jia et al., JNCI Cancer Spectrum 2020 (doi:10.1093/jncics/pkaa021). Verified at the Catalog REST record 2026-08-11. TWO CAVEATS THAT MAKE THIS A CITATION AND NOT A TARGET, both from the record itself: the model is fitted WITH COVARIATES - 'family history of cancer (in first-degree relatives), genotyping array' - which a bare weighted dot product does not have; and the cohort was 'missing 25 variants (8%) based on availability of variants in the cohort', so the published figure is for 288 of the 313 variants, not all of them. This replaced PGS000001's C-index 0.628 (PPM017270) when the score changed. That figure was a Harrell's C-index over censored follow-up, not an AUROC, and the two are not directly comparable - a C-index is computed over time-to-event pairs and an AUROC over a fixed case/control split. PGS000004 publishes a genuine AUROC, so the switch also removes that comparability problem rather than only changing the number.
not_measured.reason: 1000 Genomes is a reference panel with no breast-cancer case/control status. AUROC requires a phenotyped cohort, so the published figure is carried as a citation, not as a measurement from this run: 0.633 (AUROC (European ancestry)).

Measured across all 28 AUROC records for this score on 2026-08-11, not taken from a range quoted elsewhere - a first attempt at this line read the first page of results only and put the ceiling at 0.6573, which is a real record but not the maximum. European records span 0.5877-0.668 over 22 entries; the largest cohort is PPM012918 at n=5,328,392 with 0.665. genomics.notes: Not a neural network, and presenting a genomic foundation model as a PRS method would be the most obvious credibility hole available. Evaluation must be stratified by genetic ancestry, and what is measured here is a distribution shift, NOT an AUROC drop: an earlier revision of this note called it an AUROC drop, but 1000 Genomes is a reference panel carrying no breast-cancer case/control status, so no AUROC is computable from it and genomics_prs.py records auroc=null rather than inventing one. PGS000004 (PRS313) is Mavaddat et al. (AJHG 2018), 313 variants - not PRS-CS or LDpred2, which are Bayesian-shrinkage methods this score does not use. An earlier architecture string named that family and contradicted this project's own training script. Until Round 31 this page ran PGS000001, the 77-variant Mavaddat 2015 score selected by genome-wide significance (P<5e-8); the switch is recorded because the variant count and the baseline both changed with it. The finding is the by_super_population.*.frac_above_global_cut rows listed above: one globally-set high-risk cut flags a far larger share of AFR than of EUR, a gap driven by allele-frequency differences rather than by risk. Read those rows, not this sentence - they are recomputed on every training run, so no figure quoted in prose here can drift away from them. The published European AUROC baseline comes from a phenotyped cohort that is access-controlled, which is why it cannot be reproduced on this page.

medical_fl.notes: Trained to test a published claim rather than to win one. MedMNIST v2 reports ResNet-50 at AUC 0.857 against ResNet-18's 0.901 on this corpus, so the expected outcome is that the larger model scores LOWER, and it is reported either way. It replaces a DenseNet-121 entry that named a dataset with no loader, no fetch command and no artefact directory, and linked a Hugging Face repo that did not exist. Architectures benchmarked only ImageNet-pretrained (AlexNet, VGG16, DenseNet-121, EfficientNet-B4 in MedMNIST+) are deliberately absent: this project dropped ImageNet weights over redistribution terms, so their published numbers are not comparable to a from-scratch run.

achieved.baseline_gap_note: This scores far below the 0.901 ResNet-18 baseline. The reason is representational rather than cryptographic: 3,226 parameters over a 14x14 input is a REPRESENTATION choice, not a feasibility limit - and this note said 'a CKKS-feasibility budget' until Round 32, which overstated how forced it was. Kim et al. (arXiv:2506.15258) do HE chest-X-ray inference on a VQGAN latent at downsampling factor 8 rather than on pixels, so the alternative to downsampling 28->14 is re-representing the input. The browser already runs onnxruntime-web, so such an encoder would run locally in plaintext with no privacy loss. Recorded as the sixth falsifiable trigger in the additional-model decision in docs/deliverable-verification.md, not acted on - and note that f=8 on a 28x28 input gives 3.5x3.5, so the transfer is the open measurement rather than a citation. This sentence claimed the trigger existed for two rounds while the table held five rows and none of them was this one; the trigger was written, and the decision moved to a tracked file so the claim can be checked. Round 24 found it had been WORSE than that - a constant predictor, emitting one class for all 156 test images, with accuracy 0.730769 exactly equal to the majority-class rate and AUC 0.354, below random. It was invisible because the registry declared `auc` while the record stored `accuracy`, and because this student had neither protection its teacher already had: class-weighted loss and AUC-based model selection. Both were added. Read `n_classes_predicted` and `majority_class_rate` beside the score - an accuracy equal to the majority rate is the signature of a model that learned nothing. Workings: references/medical-student-collapse-investigation.md.
achieved.metric_note: Two metrics are recorded and they answer different questions. `auc` is the registry's declared headline and is what the published baseline compares against. `student_metric`/`teacher_metric` are accuracy, because fidelity compares DECISIONS and a decision has no score to rank - so agreement and metric_delta are necessarily computed on a decision metric. Do not read the accuracy against the AUC baseline.

achieved.baseline_gap_note: Read n_events_scored before comparing this to the baseline. The scored test window holds THREE labelled anomaly events, not the 320 that n_anomaly_intervals counts over the whole timeline - the annotated anomalies sit earlier in the mission, so a temporal split leaves almost nothing to score. Both recorded values decompose uniquely on three events: 0.714286 is tp=1 fp=0 fn=2 and 0.454545 is tp=1 fp=1 fn=2, so the 0.26 swing between two identical-config runs is ONE extra false-alarm run. The detector flags 2 points out of 441,600. Three protocol gaps to the citation remain open and are stated rather than closed: ESA-ADB multiplies event precision by the time-level TNR (recorded here as corrected_event_wise_f0_5), it splits each mission in half where this tests on the last 30 percent, and its lightweight test partition holds 65 events against 3 here. Workings: references/satellite-event-count-investigation.md.
achieved.dataset: ESA Anomaly Dataset (ESA-ADB), Mission1 lightweight channels 41-46
achieved.metric_note: Event-wise F-beta at beta=0.5 under the overlap rule, which is what ESA-ADB and Telemanom report. Telemanom's widely-quoted 0.71 is F0.5, not F1. point_adjusted_f1 is shown only to expose how much point adjustment inflates: Kim et al. (AAAI 2022) show that under point adjustment even a random anomaly score can reach state-of-the-art. Only labels whose ESA-ADB Category is 'Anomaly' count as positives; the 690 annotated rare *nominal* events do not.
achieved.sample_size_note: Read n_events_scored before comparing this to published_lightweight_f0_5. The denominator of an event-wise metric is EVENTS, and a temporal split of this corpus leaves very few of them in the scored window: 320 labelled intervals over the whole timeline reduce to a handful inside the test window, because the annotated anomalies are concentrated earlier in the mission. The recorded score is therefore a small-sample figure and one event either way moves it by tenths - it is NOT comparable to a published benchmark computed over the full annotated set, however similar the two decimals look. The number is reported as measured rather than reweighted, and the sample size is reported beside it so the comparison is not made silently.

That number is real and correctly attributed, but Table 2 scores ALL EVENTS excluding communication gaps, i.e. anomalies PLUS annotated rare nominal events, so it was the wrong comparator and the lenient one. Verified against the paper (arXiv:2406.17826 v2) in Round 24. THREE protocol differences remain and none of them are closed by changing the number: (1) ESA-ADB's metric multiplies event precision by the TIME-LEVEL true-negative rate, which is why most of its baselines read <0.001 - this project records that corrected value as `corrected_event_wise_f0_5` beside the uncorrected one; (2) ESA-ADB splits each mission in half, this project tests on the last 30 percent; (3) ESA-ADB's Mission1 lightweight test partition holds 65 annotated events of which 29 are anomalies, against 3 in the window scored here. So this remains an indicative target, and the sample-size gap is roughly tenfold.

satellite_comms.notes: Report event-wise F0.5, never point-adjusted F1. Always run a trivial baseline alongside: windowed isolation forest wins the ESA-ADB Mission2 lightweight subset outright. RETRACTION, Round 19: a Round 18 note here claimed this forecaster was about 22x WORSE than persistence. That was a measurement error of ours, not a property of the model -- the probe resampled at 60s while the model is trained at 300s (see `resample` in the achieved record). Re-measured at the trained cadence, next-step MAE is 0.0314 on the evaluation split against 0.0897 for persistence, i.e. the model is about 2.9x BETTER; 0.40x / 0.35x / 0.38x on train / test / whole series. Preprocessing for any evaluation must be read from this record rather than hardcoded, which is now what scripts/prep_model_inputs.py does. SEPARATE AND STILL OPEN: event-wise F0.5 does not reproduce across identical-config retrains -- 0.4545 here against the 0.714286 recorded -- while point-adjusted F1 does (0.9937 vs 0.9945) and the isolation-forest baseline reproduces exactly (0.000248). Treat the event-wise figure as a single draw from a wide distribution, which is the instability arXiv:2607.11969 (2026-07) describes for overlap-based metrics.

satellite_comms.notes: The one published model with no browser evaluation sample, and the reason is the metric rather than the weights. Round 21 gave the other three students samples; this one is scored on event-wise F0.5, which is defined over contiguous runs of a timeline and cannot be computed from a shuffled set of independent rows -- which is exactly what the browser evaluator scores. Shipping a per-row metric instead would verify a number nobody published for it. It needs no scaler, unlike the other three: scripts/train/satellite_telemanom.py fits it on raw `flat_te` (the last 8 timesteps x 6 channels), so the absent `input` block in its weights.json is correct rather than the omission it looks like. metric.baseline_source: Architecture showcase, not a performance claim. On THIS project's synthetic telemetry neither quantum model beats the classical random forest (RF macro F1 0.987 vs variational QNN 0.467). Published results are MIXED, not uniformly below a random forest -- an earlier revision of this note claimed they were, and the very paper cited here contradicts it: Al-Kuwari et al. (arXiv:2509.14282) Table VIII reports a hybrid QLSTM at 94.7% accuracy / 94.7% F1 against their own random-forest baseline on the same generated data. What remains well-founded is caution about evaluation quality rather than a universal ranking: arXiv:2512.05069 was withdrawn by its own authors for evaluation that was 'insufficient to fully support the conclusions'. That single withdrawal is thin support for a field-wide claim, so the anchor is now a survey: Kaissar, Bou Nassif & Bouridane, Future Internet 18(5):234 (2026-04-27, CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.3390/fi18050234), systematic to January 2026, finds that 'most current approaches rely on simulated quantum environments and legacy datasets, while evaluation practices remain inconsistent across studies' - active but methodologically early, which is a different and better-founded statement than 'worse than a random forest'. The Al-Kuwari paper is now peer-reviewed: IET Quantum Communication 7(1), DOI 10.1049/qtc2.70028 (2026-02-23). And the nearest strong 2026 result is CLASSICAL, which corroborates the framing here - but it is a DIFFERENT problem and Round 46 stopped calling it the same one. IACR ePrint 2026/1282 reaches 96.9% recall / 97.6% precision with physics-aware temporal features plus XGBoost against 17.3% for static QBER thresholding - but its abstract, read at source, is entanglement-based BBM92, a 24-dimensional feature space over 30-second sliding windows, binary detection of blended sub-threshold attacks on simulated FSO telemetry. This model classifies 8 BB84 attack TYPES from per-session physical observables. Neither the protocol, the label space nor the feature space matches, so it is an anchor, not a baseline.

achieved.baseline_gap_note: There is no baseline number to have a gap to, and that is a deliberate registry decision rather than a missing measurement: the two figures usually quoted for this corpus (99.61% for a CNN, 99.71% for a hybrid quantum-classical Quan-ConvCNN, Wang/Fok/Thing) are ACCURACIES, and this model is judged on macro F1, so putting them in `baseline` would render an accuracy beside a macro F1 as though the two were the same scale. WHAT THE GAP ACTUALLY IS, now that it has been measured properly. This model scores about 0.9829 accuracy with every row identifier and every host fingerprint dropped, so it sits about 1.3 points below those published accuracies rather than the 24 points it sat below them last round. Against the 9-class multiclass figure that is directly comparable in task - BiTAD, Future Internet 17(11) 482, accuracy 0.9047 - it is above, though on its own split rather than a shared one, so that is an anchor and not a head-to-head. THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERS. Round 49 recorded that restoring the corpus's integer row counters reproduces the published range and implied the published range was therefore explained by them. The first half is still measured true here and is recorded every run as `leak_counterfactual_accuracy`. The second half does not follow and is withdrawn: 0.9829 is reachable on this corpus with no identifiers at all, using one additional flow statistic (`IdleTime`) that Combined.csv does not carry, so most of the gap Round 49 attributed to leakage was its own choice of export. What the counterfactual shows is what a row counter is worth, which is a statement about this corpus and not about anyone's paper.

achieved.framing: Real 5G network traffic, 9 attack classes, 47 flow-statistic features. This is a NETWORK-LAYER model and a different task from the QKD-layer classifier on the same page - no shared labels, no shared features, so the two scores are not a comparison. IT IS FITTED ON THE FIELDS-PRESERVED EXPORT (113 columns) AND WAS FITTED ON Combined.csv (52) UNTIL ROUND 50, which is the single most important thing to know about the numbers here: the same rows and the same classes, but the narrow export omits `IdleTime` and that one column is worth 22 points of accuracy. `idle_time_ablation` re-measures this every run by refitting without it, and the result reproduces what this model used to score. Two controls are recorded beside the headline and both are worth more than the headline. `idle_time_ablation` says the old weakness was a choice of export, not a property of the corpus. `leak_counterfactual_accuracy` says that restoring four integer row counters takes accuracy to about 0.9997, which is not a better model but a leak.

idle_time_ablation.what_this_means: Removing `IdleTime` ALONE costs essentially the same accuracy as removing all six columns Combined.csv omits, and both land on the score this model published while it was fitted on Combined.csv. The other five - `Dir`, `Flgs`, `TcpOpt`, `sVlan`, `dVlan` - are worth 0.0006 accuracy between them. So the model's former weakness was one absent flow statistic, not the corpus and not the method. THAT IS REDUNDANCY AND NOT EMPTINESS, stated because the shorter version would be false. Two of those five are individually strong - `Dir` scores one-vs-rest AUC 0.9811 on ICMPFlood and `TcpOpt` 0.9433 on SlowrateDoS, both above the 0.90 threshold `single_feature_leak_check` uses, and both appear in its flagged list. What the ablation shows is that the other 41 columns already carry what they carry. `IdleTime` IS NOT AN IDENTIFIER and the distinction is the same one `leak_counterfactual_*` exists to draw: it takes 17 distinct integer values over 1,215,890 rows, so it cannot encode a row position, and it separates `SlowrateDoS` - an attack defined by holding a connection idle - at one-vs-rest AUC 0.9574. A row counter that scores that well describes where a row sits in a file. This describes what the traffic did.

linear_baseline.what_it_is: multinomial logistic regression on the 37 NUMERIC features only, standardised, fitted directly rather than distilled. The 10 ordinal codes are excluded because their integer order is nominal and a linear model would read it as a magnitude. Recorded as the classical floor and as a feasibility probe for a future CKKS-linear tier: it predicts 9 of 9 classes, so a linear student on this corpus does not collapse the way an 8-class one nearly does elsewhere in this project.

achieved.metric_note: THE TWO NUMBERS STILL READ THE OPPOSITE WAY ROUND FROM EVERY OTHER MODEL IN THIS PROJECT, and the refit onto the wide export did NOT fix that - it shrank it. Everywhere else here the aggregate flatters and the per-class figure exposes it, which is why `aggregate_accuracy` is rendered as the companion 'shown so the gap is visible'. On this corpus macro F1 is still the OPTIMISTIC number and aggregate accuracy still the PESSIMISTIC one. What changed is the size of the disagreement: macro F1 minus accuracy was 0.1655 on the narrow export (0.9263 against 0.7608) and is about 0.0121 now (0.9950 against 0.9829). THE MECHANISM IS UNCHANGED, which is the part a reader is most likely to get wrong. It is not that a small class now drags the macro average - the smallest class, ICMPFlood at 289 test rows, scores 1.0000 and lifts it. It is the same two majority classes as before: Benign at 39.3% of rows and UDPFlood at 37.6% are the only pair that confuses at all, they carry 77% of the test set between them, so accuracy is dominated by them while a macro average over 9 classes is carried by the seven scoring 0.9999 or better. Adding `IdleTime` separated that pair almost completely rather than changing which pair it is. The residual is one directional confusion - UDPFlood predicted as Benign - and it is 1.71% of the test set against 23.92% before. Read `per_class_f1` and it is visible directly: the two lowest entries are Benign and UDPFlood, and every other class is at or above 0.9999. Neither figure is the flattering one to quote alone.
achieved.sample_size_note: Trained and scored on the whole of 5G-NIDD BTS1_BTS2_fields_preserved.csv - 1,215,890 flows, stratified 75/25 at seed 42, so the test split is 303,973 rows and every class keeps its corpus proportion. Row for row this is the same corpus as Combined.csv, which this model used until Round 50; only the column count differs, 113 against 52. No subsampling and no class rebalancing: `ICMPFlood` is 1,155 rows in the corpus and 289 in the test split, which is small but is the real prevalence, and resampling it would report a per-class F1 for a distribution the deployed model never sees. The browser evaluation sample is a different matter and is NOT proportional - see the note in eval_sample.json, which states its per-class floor and why its macro F1 is not this one.

single_feature_leak_check.what_this_means: One-vs-rest rank-AUC per feature per class, at the 0.90 threshold scripts/prep_model_inputs.py already publishes against, measured AFTER all 66 drops. A LARGE NUMBER HERE IS EXPECTED ON THIS CORPUS AND IS NOT THE LEAK THIS MODEL IS ABOUT. The attacks are generated by distinct tools against distinct services, so a scan, a SYN flood and a slow-rate HTTP attack genuinely differ in TTL, packet rate, TCP window and ACK timing - these are the flow statistics an intrusion detector is supposed to use. The check's own docstring anticipates the case and warns rather than failing. The distinction that matters is against `leak_counterfactual_*`: `Unnamed: 0`, `Rank`, `Seq` and `Offset` cleared the same threshold while being bookkeeping columns that carry no information about the traffic at all, which is why those four are dropped and these are kept. `IdleTime` is in this list and is the case that shows the rule is not circular - it clears the threshold on SlowrateDoS, it is the single most valuable column in the corpus by `idle_time_ablation`, and it takes 17 distinct integer values over 1.2 million rows, so no amount of it can address a row. Recorded rather than described so the distinction is checkable.

metric.baseline_source: Two published figures on 5G-NIDD are usually quoted - Wang, Fok & Thing report 99.61% accuracy for a CNN and 99.71% for a hybrid quantum-classical Quan-ConvCNN - and BOTH are accuracies, which is why no number appears in `baseline`. Three caveats. (1) Those are hybrid quantum-classical results with a 0.10-point spread, and the authors' own claim is about generalisation to UNSEEN attacks rather than about the headline; `references/REFERENCES.md` WS2 records this. (2) Accuracy is the wrong comparator on a corpus whose two majority classes are 39.3% and 37.6% of the rows. (3) MEASURED HERE: an identical gradient-boosted model reaches accuracy 0.9997 with the corpus's integer row counters restored, so the published range is reproducible from row identifiers alone. ROUND 50 CORRECTED WHAT THAT THIRD POINT WAS TAKEN TO MEAN. It was written when this model scored 0.7610 and read as evidence that the published figures probably leaned on those counters, on the unstated premise that nothing else could close a 24-point gap. Something else could. Refitted on the corpus's 113-column export with every identifier and every host fingerprint dropped, the same configuration scores 0.9829 - about 1.3 points below the published accuracies rather than 24 - and the column that closes the gap is one flow statistic, `IdleTime`, which the 52-column export does not carry. The leak measurement stands as a fact about row counters. The insinuation about the papers does not, and is withdrawn. These figures are an anchor and not a target that has been beaten or missed.

telecom_ids.notes: NETWORK-LAYER flow classification on real 5G traffic. This is a DIFFERENT TASK from the QKD-layer attack classifier on this same page, with zero overlap in label space or feature space, so neither score is the other's baseline. REFITTED IN ROUND 50 ON A WIDER EXPORT OF THE SAME CORPUS, which is the fact that explains every number here. It trained on `Combined.csv` (52 columns) and scored accuracy 0.7608; it now trains on `BTS1_BTS2_fields_preserved.csv` (113 columns) and scores about 0.9829. The rows are identical and the method is unchanged. One column does all of it: `IdleTime`, a flow statistic the narrow export omits. Removing it alone from the wide fit returns the model to 0.7616, and that ablation is re-measured on every run as `idle_time_ablation`. It is not an identifier - 17 distinct integer values over 1.2 million rows - and it separates SlowrateDoS, an attack defined by idling, at one-vs-rest AUC 0.9574. READ THE TWO NUMBERS THE OTHER WAY ROUND FROM EVERYWHERE ELSE IN THIS PROJECT - STILL. Every other model here reports an aggregate that flatters and a per-class figure that does not. On this corpus macro F1 is the OPTIMISTIC number and aggregate accuracy the pessimistic one, and the refit shrank that inversion without removing it: the gap was 0.1655 (0.9263 macro F1 against 0.7608 accuracy) and is about 0.0121 (0.9950 against 0.9829). The mechanism is the same one as before, not a new one - Benign and UDPFlood are 39.3% and 37.6% of the rows and remain the only pair that confuses, so accuracy is dominated by them while the macro average is carried by seven classes at 0.9999 or better. The residual error is 1.71% of the test split against 23.92% before, and it is one direction: UDPFlood predicted as Benign. THE LEAK COUNTERFACTUAL IS STILL RECORDED EVERY RUN and its claim is now narrower. Restoring the corpus's integer row identifiers takes accuracy to about 0.9997, the same shape of result Engelen et al. (WTMC 2021) produced for CIC-IDS2017. Round 49 read that as an explanation for the published 99.6-99.7% figures; it is not, because 0.9829 is reachable here with no identifiers at all -- see M_NIDD's baseline_source, which withdraws that reading.

achieved.metric_note: Read `n_classes_predicted` before `macro_f1`. A linear student that stops predicting a class scores 0 on it by construction, and macro F1 then averages in a zero that looks like poor discrimination rather than an absent output - this repo's own QNN carries exactly that defect and is documented as doing so, so the check is not hypothetical. `agreement` is recorded but is NOT evidence the minority classes survived: agreement on the finance student rose from 0.884 to 0.947 across a change that left minority-class F1 unmoved, which is why per-class F1 is the headline here and the aggregate is a companion.

metric.baseline_source: Architecture showcase, not a performance claim. On THIS project's synthetic telemetry neither quantum model beats the classical random forest (RF macro F1 0.987 vs variational QNN 0.467). Published results are MIXED, not uniformly below a random forest -- an earlier revision of this note claimed they were, and the very paper cited here contradicts it: Al-Kuwari et al. (arXiv:2509.14282) Table VIII reports a hybrid QLSTM at 94.7% accuracy / 94.7% F1 against their own random-forest baseline on the same generated data. What remains well-founded is caution about evaluation quality rather than a universal ranking: arXiv:2512.05069 was withdrawn by its own authors for evaluation that was 'insufficient to fully support the conclusions'. That single withdrawal is thin support for a field-wide claim, so the anchor is now a survey: Kaissar, Bou Nassif & Bouridane, Future Internet 18(5):234 (2026-04-27, CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.3390/fi18050234), systematic to January 2026, finds that 'most current approaches rely on simulated quantum environments and legacy datasets, while evaluation practices remain inconsistent across studies' - active but methodologically early, which is a different and better-founded statement than 'worse than a random forest'. The Al-Kuwari paper is now peer-reviewed: IET Quantum Communication 7(1), DOI 10.1049/qtc2.70028 (2026-02-23). And the nearest strong 2026 result is CLASSICAL, which corroborates the framing here - but it is a DIFFERENT problem and Round 46 stopped calling it the same one. IACR ePrint 2026/1282 reaches 96.9% recall / 97.6% precision with physics-aware temporal features plus XGBoost against 17.3% for static QBER thresholding - but its abstract, read at source, is entanglement-based BBM92, a 24-dimensional feature space over 30-second sliding windows, binary detection of blended sub-threshold attacks on simulated FSO telemetry. This model classifies 8 BB84 attack TYPES from per-session physical observables. Neither the protocol, the label space nor the feature space matches, so it is an anchor, not a baseline.

telecom_ids.notes: Distilled from telecom_ids.qml's PROBABILITIES, not its argmax: on 8 classes the argmax discards exactly the minority-class signal macro F1 is computed from, and hard-label distillation is a defect this project has already made once. Read n_classes_predicted before macro_f1 - a linear student that stops emitting a class scores 0 on it by construction, which reads as poor discrimination rather than an absent output.
